title: Count Ways to Decode a Digit String
statement: A field radio operator receives messages as strings of digits. Each letter was encoded before transmission as its alphabet position: 'A' -> "1", 'B' -> "2", ..., 'Z' -> "26". Given the received digit string code, return the number of distinct letter sequences (an int) it could decode to. A digit may be used either on its own (only "1" through "9"; a lone "0" maps to nothing) or paired with the digit after it as a two-digit token, which is valid only when it reads as a number from 10 to 26. Every digit of code must be consumed by exactly one token. If no complete decoding exists (for example a leading '0', or a '0' that cannot attach to a preceding 1 or 2), return 0. The empty string counts as exactly one decoding: the empty message.
hints: The number of decodings of the first i digits depends only on decodings of slightly shorter prefixes. Which two prefixes, and does that recurrence look familiar?
Let dp[i] = decodings of the first i digits, with dp[0] = 1 for the empty prefix. This is Fibonacci-style counting, but each of the two additions needs a validity guard.

For each i: add dp[i-1] only if code[i-1] is '1'-'9' (a lone '0' decodes to nothing), and add dp[i-2] only if code[i-2:i] reads as 10-26 (so '06' and '27' do not count as pairs). Return dp[n]; unreachable states stay 0.
